title: Gaptoothed
html_source:
The eponymous title character of Yeats' play Cathleen ni Houlihan, which Joyce is referencing here, is a poor old woman. Thus, the adjective is, first of all, used disparagingly. With Kathleen symbolising Ireland as a whole, the allusion gains more poignancy.

Beyond that, the county town Wicklow, that was mentioned in the preceding sentence, is called Cill Mhantáin in Irish, meaning “church of the toothless one”. The origin of the name is rich in folklore:

“Saint Patrick and some followers are said to have tried to land on Travailahawk beach, to the south of the harbour. Hostile locals attacked them, causing one of Patrick’s party to lose his front teeth. Manntach (toothless one), as he became known, was undeterred and returned to the town, eventually founding a church.” (See: Wikipedia)

The name could, however, also be a toponym and refer to the St. Patrick’s Church in Wicklow, which is said to resemble a gappy set of teeth.

Nevertheless, Wicklow and Ireland are superimposed upon each other via the corresponding adjective “gaptoothed”.
